items.t: “Very Bad” News for Alibaba: Nvidia’s B300 Servers Now Cost Nearly $3 Million in China.
sum: - Eight Nvidia B300 chips for a server now list for nearly $3 million in China, more than five times the U.S. price of a B300 server.
- Riedel Research's David Riedel says that's "very bad" for Alibaba, as Washington moves to curb its offshore access to Nvidia chips.
- Alibaba's capex nearly quadrupled in two years while its EBIT margin fell to 6.2%.

Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) chips just hit a price in China that should worry Alibaba (BABA:NYSE) shareholders far more than Nvidia's. CNBC Beijing bureau chief Eunice Yoon reported the number from Chinese listings on Squawk on the Street on Nov. 12:
"The price of a set of eight Blackwell B300 chips for a server is now at nearly $3 million. This is up five times from May and nearly six times higher than the official U.S. price of $550,000."

David Riedel, founder and president of Riedel Research, told Closing Bell who that hurts: "I don't think it has a huge impact on NVIDIA's business… But for the Chinese, for Alibaba in particular, it's very bad."
He's right about Nvidia. The B300 is restricted from sale in China, so none of that markup reaches it.

items.t: Alibaba stock: T-Head IPO advances without assured allocation
sum: Alibaba Group's T-Head chip subsidiary has advanced toward a Hong Kong listing, adding a fresh corporate-development angle for investors ahead of the group's November 19 results. The announcement dated November 10 said T-Head had confidentially submitted a listing application for H shares on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange Main Board.

According to PPC Land, the Hong Kong exchange granted Alibaba a waiver from the requirement to provide existing shareholders with an assured entitlement to T-Head shares. Investors who want exposure to the chip unit would therefore have to participate in the Hong Kong public offering or institutional placing on the same terms as other eligible investors, or buy after a listing.

The proposed offering is expected to include a Hong Kong public tranche and a placing for institutional and professional investors. The size and structure of the offering, Alibaba's post-listing stake, valuation and timetable remain open. T-Head is expected to remain an Alibaba subsidiary if the transaction proceeds.

The listing remains subject to approval from the Listing Committee of the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, completion of the required filing with China's securities regulator and final decisions by Alibaba and T-Head. The company has given no listing date, so the plan remains a process milestone rather than a completed transaction.

Alibaba Group Holding Ltd Stock (BABA) Moved Down by 3.67% on Nov 9: Key Drivers Unveiled
sum: Alibaba Group Holding Ltd (BABA) moved down by 3.67%. The Software & IT Services sector is up by 2.09%. The company underperformed the industry. Top 3 stocks by turnover in the sector: Alphabet Inc Class A (GOOGL) up 1.91%; Meta Platforms Inc (META) up 5.15%; Microsoft Corp (MSFT) up 2.73%.

Alibaba faced notable downward pressure during the trading session, driven by a confluence of intensifying domestic e-commerce competition, macroeconomic headwinds across Chinese consumer markets, and institutional de-risking ahead of upcoming corporate earnings and peak promotional milestones.

A primary catalyst weighing on sentiment is the heightened competitive friction surrounding the annual Singles Day shopping period. Aggressive promotional campaigns and extensive merchant subsidies across Taobao and Tmall reflect an industry-wide price war against rival platforms, including PDD Holdings and Douyin. While promotional intensity aids gross merchandise volume traction, institutional investors remain concerned that elevated customer acquisition spending and return logistics costs will compress core merchant margins and dilute short-term operational profitability.

Broader macroeconomic conditions have compounded this cautious outlook. Lingering softness in domestic consumer discretionary spending and uneven household sentiment continue to cloud the trajectory of retail recovery in China. At the same time, fluctuations in the offshore yuan against a resilient U.S. dollar have created incremental currency drag on U.S.-listed American Depositary Receipts. The resulting macro overhang has limited multiple expansion, prompting multi-asset funds to temper exposure to Chinese tech equities.

Institutional portfolio adjustments also contributed to intraday weakness. Capital allocators have increasingly adopted defensive positioning ahead of Alibaba's pending financial results, seeking clarity on monetization rates, cloud division growth, and the execution of ongoing artificial intelligence initiatives. Until clearer evidence of sustained margin preservation and a broader domestic consumption rebound emerges, the stock is likely to remain sensitive to macroeconomic data releases and headline geopolitical risk.

sum: Alibaba's US-listed shares finished Friday up 2.0%, riding a broader rebound in American technology and AI stocks that the Associated Press linked to a recovery following a two-day selloff. The advance came one day after the Chinese e-commerce and cloud group had already joined a wider rally among Hong Kong tech names.

That Thursday session saw the Hang Seng Tech Index climb 5%, according to Reuters, as investors welcomed reduced uncertainty following the US midterm elections and a strong showing on Wall Street. The twin gains left Alibaba tracking sector momentum on both sides of the Pacific.

Research desks have been adding to the positive tone. Wei Fang of Mizuho Securities raised his price target to $200 from $195 on Tuesday while reiterating a buy rating. Citi's Alicia Yap had reaffirmed her own buy call and $193 target on November 2.

Media coverage earlier in the week also flagged two company-specific threads: reports of planned central bank discussions in China aimed at improving credit support for share buybacks and stake increases — with Alibaba named among the beneficiaries, though no additional financing had been announced — and the planned integration of Alibaba's Qwen model into Apple's offering for the Chinese market. Roughly a week earlier, reports had pointed to a December launch of Apple Intelligence for consumers incorporating the Alibaba model.

On the corporate front, Alibaba said on November 2 that it will supply cloud and AI technology for Dakar 2026, the first Youth Olympic Games to be held in Africa. The infrastructure is intended to support event operations and enable AI functions, with the private cloud to be handed over to Senegal after the Games for use as a national cloud platform.

Alibaba also secured a partial legal victory on October 26, when Reuters reported that a US federal court had issued a preliminary injunction against certain restrictions on Pentagon contracts. Under the ruling, the government may not exclude companies from contracts solely because they, their parent companies or subsidiaries maintain business relationships with lobbyists holding an Alibaba mandate. The decision did not remove Alibaba from the Pentagon list.

Bloomberg cited a report Sunday from Cailian, which cited people in the industry. Bloomberg said a state-backed effort would add to steps China took last month to stabilize its equity market. sum: Shares of Alibaba jumped around 3% in Hong Kong on Tuesday after the Chinese technology giant unveiled a new artificial intelligence chip and plans to sharply expand its data center footprint, stepping up its bet on the infrastructure powering the AI boom.

At its cloud unit's annual flagship Apsara Conference in Hangzhou, Alibaba introduced the Zhenwu V900, its next-generation AI chip that it said delivers three times the performance of its predecessor, the Zhenwu M890 released in May.

The company also announced plans to expand Alibaba Cloud's global data center capacity to more than 20 gigawatts by 2032 as part of a broader roadmap spanning chips, cloud infrastructure and AI models.

The announcements underscore Alibaba's growing push into the machinery behind the AI boom, amid a flurry of AI infrastructure investments by its Western tech peers as the race for computing power intensifies.

Earlier this month, Nvidia outlined plans to work with Australian partners to support up to 2 gigawatts of AI infrastructure in the country by 2027, while Meta in July unveiled plans for its first data center in Canada, a 1-gigawatt facility in Alberta expected to cost about $9 billion and take up to three years to complete.

Alibaba's new Zhenwu AI chip is scheduled for mass production and commercial release in the first quarter of 2027. Its existing Zhenwu chips are already used by more than 650 customers across industries including automotive, finance, energy and manufacturing.
The company also said its next-generation Qwen 4 model is currently in training and outlined plans for future Qwen 4.5 and Qwen 5 model series.

So I was checking my portfolio the other day and noticed $Alibaba (BABA.US)$ sliding hard , enough that I stopped scrolling and actually asked $Futu Holdings Ltd (FUTU.US)$'s AI to break down what was going on, especially since I've been holding this position for a while. Here's what it dug up, and honestly it gave me a lot more clarity than just staring at the red numbers.

Now let's get into what actually happened according to MooMoo's AI, because it's not as scary as the headlines make it sound. The recent crash was about 17.4% from the August high of $132.32. If you zoom out to the 52 week high near $190.92, the drop is a much bigger 42.8% So there are really 2 stories here, a sharp recent slide and a longer, deeper drawdown that's been building for a while.

What caused it? This wasn't some random China tech panic. It was mostly Alibaba specific Revenue actually grew 8.6% year on year to about RMB268.95 billion, so this was never a demand problem . The issue was what it cost to get that growth. Net profit fell about 75% to RMB10.4 billion, and adjusted net profit of RMB20.72 billion missed what analysts were expecting by a wide margin . Adjusted earnings per ADS dropped 42% to $1.26, versus the $1.85 the street wanted . Quarterly capex jumped 75% to RMB67.68 billion, and free cash flow actually went negative, an outflow of RMB44.67 billion . Then just after that report, Alibaba announced a share placement of around 710 million new shares to raise about $10.2 billion, mainly to fund more AI infrastructure . That dilution news hit the Hong Kong listed shares by 8.5% and dragged the ADRs down too.

If you break down the causes, it's pretty clearly a company specific story rather than a macro one. The earnings miss, the heavy AI and quick commerce spending, and the dilution from the placement were all Alibaba specific issues. Broader tech weakness and softer consumer spending in the sector added some pressure, but they were background noise, not the main trigger. There wasn't even any major new regulatory action behind this, which is actually a bit of a relief given Alibaba's history.

Alibaba (BABA) gave analysts one event to react to, and they walked away pointing in opposite directions. On September 7, Bernstein’s Robin Zhu cut his price target to $165 from $180 while keeping an Outperform rating. The same morning, BofA’s Joyce Ju raised her target to $175 from $172 and kept her Buy. Both were staring at the identical fact: Alibaba had just sold $10.2 billion of new stock to fund AI infrastructure, three days after telling investors it held $30.7 billion in net cash.

The argument is narrower: whether raising equity at a discount, while free cash flow bleeds, is disciplined capital allocation or a warning about returns on all this spending. The stock has round-tripped back to about $109 after falling roughly 10% on the placement, so the market has not settled it either.

Zhu wrote that with Alibaba holding $30.7 billion of net cash, the deal “diluted the credibility of management’s ROI claims,” yet his own analysis “mostly supports management’s claims on payback on capex.” He built a data center model around Alibaba’s Zhenwu 810E chip, showing a roughly three-year payback, tightening toward 2.5 years on the newer M890. His problem was the timing and optics of funding the buildout through dilution, not the strategy.

For the June period (fiscal Q1 2027), reported August 20, revenue rose 8.6% to RMB 268.95 billion, a slight beat, while everything below the top line went the other way. Adjusted EBITDA fell 30%, GAAP net income dropped 75%, and free cash flow swung to an RMB 44.7 billion outflow as capex hit RMB 67.7 billion in a single quarter. Adjusted EPS of RMB 8.52 missed the RMB 10.82 that the Street expected. TIKR logs an 8.57% single-day drop on the August 20 earnings date, though the print-day reaction was volatile and the larger, cleaner selloff came days later on the placement.

Management is not hiding the tradeoff. CFO Toby Xu described capital allocation as running across “investments for AI + Cloud business growth, share buybacks and dividends,” with priorities that shift as conditions evolve.

Qwen3.8-Max, which is scheduled for release next week, boasts 2.4 trillion parameters, making it one of the "most powerful" AI models in the Chinese tech giant's Qwen family of AI models to date, Alibaba said. Alibaba shared results showing it delivering comparable or sometimes better scores than Anthropic's Fable 5. The model also only ranks second to Fable 5 in the Vision Arena, and fifth in the Text Arena.
It comes after domestic rival Moonshot AI released Kimi K3 earlier this month, which has 2.8 trillion parameters, making it China's largest AI model.

Meanwhile, Qwen3.8-Max can code highly autonomously for weeks with little human input, Alibaba said. In one internal test, it spent 16 days building and improving an AI coding tool by writing code, testing it, fixing errors, and refining its work on its own.

sum: BEIJING, Aug 3 (Reuters) – China’s Alibaba on Monday unveiled its largest and most capable AI model to date, sending its shares surging, while a research firm said DeepSeek’s latest product offers cut-throat pricing that is more than 100 times cheaper than Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.

The two developments highlight the rapid pace of advancement in artificial intelligence by Chinese tech firms, which are locked in a fierce and fast-moving battle to build more powerful systems without making them prohibitively expensive to run.
Both models — Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-Max and DeepSeek’s V4-Flash — underline Chinese commitment to open-weight models as the firms seek to gain traction among developers globally.
“Chinese AI companies have found an important market. Many business workflows do not need the industry’s very best model,” said Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at research firm Omdia.
“They need models that are good enough, affordable, transparent and accessible, and open-weight models help meet that demand.”

With an open-weight model, the underlying learned settings that allow developers to run or adapt the system are available for download. By contrast, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have closed-source models.
Alibaba’s new Qwen3.8-Max immediately shot up leaderboards assessing the capabilities of AI models after being unveiled on Monday, helping its shares jump 7% in Hong Kong trade.

Kimi K3 is the largest open-weight AI model released to date, according to Moonshot. The model places below Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 and OpenAI's GPT 5.6 Sol in overall rankings, yet beat Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT 5.5 across coding and general agent evaluations. Arena blind evaluations showed developers choosing Kimi K3 ahead of all top U.S. models on front-end coding tasks, and K3 matched GPT 5.6 Sol when ranked across Arena's general text category, according to Axios. Rather than undercutting the market, Moonshot has positioned the API near Anthropic's mid-range price tier, distancing K3 from the steep discounts that have defined most Chinese model releases, Axios reported.

Moonshot has set July 27 as the date for publishing K3's full weights, leaving developers without the ability to self-host or alter the model in the meantime. The company said the model is available now through Kimi.com, mobile apps, and its API.

items.t: How Alibaba overcame Beijing's crackdown to become an AI giant
sum: On a cold November evening in Shanghai in 2020, the world's largest IPO was abruptly canceled by Chinese regulators.

It was Ant Group, the fintech affiliate of tech giant Alibaba. The company's founder Jack Ma, one of China's most famous billionaires, was under scrutiny for comments seemingly criticising the country's financial regulators.

Since the IPO cancelation, more than $400 billion has been wiped off Alibaba's value, even with a more recent rally. In the months after the failed public listing, Ma retreated from the public eye and Alibaba, China's biggest e-commerce player, looked down and out, with management and structure changes bearing little fruit. The moves were not characteristic of the grit the company had shown in the past and a far cry from its strong position now.
"The hallmark of Jack and his personality is that he never gave up," Brian Wong, a former Alibaba executive and author of "The Tao of Alibaba," told CNBC.

Wong features in my new show "Built for Billions," in which I explore Alibaba's most testing moments and delve into how it grew to become one of the world's biggest tech companies and one of the most advanced artificial intelligence players.

I've been covering tech for more than a decade with much of my focus centering on China. I lived in the world's second-largest economy for three years, from October 2018 to December 2021 when Alibaba was undergoing this significant shift. The company's reach cannot be overstated from its humble beginnings in 1999 as a business to business online marketplace in the early days of the internet.

Now Alibaba's business touches everything from food delivery to global e-commerce, cloud computing and artificial intelligence. items.t: Alphabet stock jumps after report of Apple’s plans to use Google AI for Siri
sum: Investing.com -- Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) stock extended gains, rising to a session high of 2.3% after Bloomberg reported that Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) plans to use a 1.2 trillion parameter Google AI model to power its upcoming Siri overhaul.

The tech giant is finalizing an agreement that would see Apple pay approximately $1 billion annually for access to Google's advanced AI technology, according to people familiar with the matter. This partnership comes after Apple reportedly evaluated several third-party models, including OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude, before selecting Google's Gemini.

Apple's decision to leverage Google's AI capabilities represents a significant vote of confidence in Alphabet's technology. The 1.2 trillion parameter model would substantially exceed the complexity of Apple's current AI systems, positioning Google as a critical partner in Apple's AI strategy.

The revamped Siri is expected to launch next spring, with Apple viewing Google's technology as an interim solution until its own AI models become sufficiently powerful. This timeline aligns with previous Bloomberg reports about Apple's AI roadmap.
